description: The European Union governs **450 million citizens**, yet the way it works often looks like a black box. Here is how a European law is really born, and who decides what.

hero.hook: 27 countries, one common rulebook: a dive into the most complex machinery in world politics.

blocks.text: The **European Union** is the most advanced experiment in union between countries in modern history. It turned a continent wrecked by war into one vast shared economic and political space.

Yet the way it works still looks like a black box to the 450 million citizens it covers. Understanding how a decision is born in Brussels makes it much easier to follow the big European debates, from the environment to digital security.

The EU runs on three institutions that have to agree with one another. The **European Council**, made up of the heads of state of the member countries, sets the broad political direction at summits, without writing any laws itself.

blocks.caption: Heads of state meet in the European Council to set the broad direction

blocks.text: The power to make laws is shared between the [[Council of the EU]], which represents the 27 governments, and the **European Parliament**, the only institution elected directly by citizens. The Parliament gives the system its democratic legitimacy.

Finally, the [[European Commission]] acts as the executive. It is the only body that can propose a new law, an exclusive right known as [[The European Commission and the monopoly of legislative initiative]]. It also makes sure countries actually follow the common rules.

The European Parliament officially sits in two cities: Brussels and Strasbourg. Every month its 705 members and all their staff take a special train to Alsace, an expensive ritual that stands for French-German reconciliation.

sections.title: Three powers, none of them in charge alone

blocks.text: A European law follows a precise path, called the ordinary legislative procedure. It all starts with a proposal from the Commission, usually after a long round of consultation with experts and [[interest groups]].

The text then goes to the Parliament and the Council of the EU. If they disagree, it shuttles back and forth between the two institutions. As a last resort, a [[conciliation committee]] meets to find a compromise.

Once adopted, the law can take two forms: a **regulation**, which applies directly and identically in every country, or a **directive**, which sets a goal but lets each country choose how to reach it.
The EU Court of Justice has had to settle some strange disputes, like the famous “banana war,” a fight over customs duties on tropical fruit that lasted more than twenty years.

sections.title: How a European law is made

blocks.text: The EU has no unlimited power: it can only act in the areas the countries handed to it. Some powers belong to it alone, such as managing the single currency or setting the rules of international trade.

blocks.caption: The European Union shares its powers across several levels of decision-making

blocks.text: Other powers are shared with the countries, such as the environment or transport. This is where the EU acts most often, but only when it can do the job better than each country on its own.

Finally, sensitive subjects like taxation, health and defense stay almost entirely in national hands, and often require the agreement of every member through [[Unanimity in the Council of the EU]]. That blockage explains why the EU can punish a big company with ease, yet sometimes struggles to agree on a common line in an international crisis.

sections.title: What the EU can do, and what it cannot

blocks.text: The picture of a Europe run by “unelected technocrats” deserves some nuance. Commission officials are appointed by democratically elected governments, then confirmed by the Parliament. The European administration is in fact small: about 60,000 staff to run a whole continent, fewer than the city of Paris employs on its own.
The sense of distance from citizens is a real problem. To answer it, the EU created the European Citizens' Initiative, which lets a million citizens ask the Commission to look at a new law.

The pandemic of 2020 was a turning point: for the first time, member countries agreed to borrow together on the financial markets, through the Next Generation EU plan. That shift from a union of markets to a union built on solidarity shows a Europe that keeps evolving.

The European Union rests on power shared between 27 countries and three institutions, none of which can decide alone. This complex system secures peace and stability, but it often reacts slowly to fast-moving crises.

title: The EU: how does it really work?
